notation.sorting: n = number of array elements. Arrays are zero-indexed. Loop bounds are inclusive and empty ranges are skipped. Bounds describe this implementation, excluding animation.
notation.pathfinding: V = grid vertices, E = traversable directed edges, K = requested paths. Moving u → v costs weight(v). The heuristic h is Manhattan distance to the goal. PATH follows parent pointers back to the start, then reverses the result. Bounds describe this implementation, excluding grid construction and animation.

Insertion Sort.note: Already sorted input takes O(n). This version inserts each item through adjacent swaps.

Quick Sort.note: Expected O(n log n) for randomly ordered distinct values. The last item is the pivot. Sorted input can cause quadratic time. The smaller partition is recursive and the larger one is handled by a loop.

Bubble Sort.note: Stops after a pass with no swaps, so already sorted input takes O(n).

Selection Sort.note: Scans the unsorted suffix on every pass, even when the input is already sorted.

Merge Sort.note: This implementation merges in place using adjacent swaps, so its worst case is quadratic. Already sorted input takes O(n log n). A buffered merge implementation would have O(n log n) worst-case time.

Comb Sort.note: Shrinks the gap by a factor of 1.3. Even sorted input still makes O(log n) gap passes, taking O(n log n) time.

A* Search.note: Uses a binary heap with priority g + h and breaks ties by smaller h. On this four-neighbor grid, weights of at least 1 make Manhattan distance consistent, so each vertex is expanded at most once and the path has minimum cost. This graph bound is not a general bound for A* tree search or inconsistent heuristics.
pseudocode: parent[v] ← none for every vertex v
frontier ← min-heap containing start, ranked by (g + h, h)
u ← pop the smallest (g + h, h)
if u = goal: return PATH(parent, goal)
for each traversable neighbor v of u:
if v is not settled and candidate < distance[v]:
push v with priority (candidate + h(v), h(v))

Greedy Best-First Search.note: Ranks the heap only by Manhattan distance to the goal. Each vertex is expanded at most once. It finds a path if one exists, but does not guarantee the fewest steps or minimum cost. This app requires weights of at least 1.

u ← pop the smallest Manhattan distance to goal

Bidirectional Dijkstra.note: Runs binary-heap Dijkstra in both directions with weights of at least 1. Reverse search from u to v costs weight(u). It stops when the two minimum queue keys cannot improve the best complete path, rather than at the first meeting.

return the joined path (include meeting only once)

Yen's K Shortest Paths.note: Yen's algorithm makes O(KV) shortest-path searches, here using A* with weights of at least 1. This implementation also compares Python list prefixes, adding O(K²V²) work to the O(KV(V + E) log V) search bound. Returns up to K distinct loopless paths in nondecreasing cost order. K is limited to 10.
